newsitem.title: USA: Voters still fear Republican agenda, hurting Dole.
newsitem.headline: Voters still fear Republican agenda, hurting Dole.

text.p: By Alan Elsner, U.S. Political Correspondent
Republican presidential nominee Bob Dole is paying a heavy price in the 1996 presidential election for the shrill rhetoric of the 1995 "Republican revolution."

In two dozen interviews with randomly selected voters from all over the country who took part in a Reuters opinion poll, it became clear that many see President Bill Clinton as defender of the environment and of valued social programmes that they fear would suffer under Dole.

Even several Republican voters said they had become alarmed last year over the policies of the Republican majority in Congress, especially the self-proclaimed apostles of the "Republican revolution" who stormed into the House of Representatives last year led by Speaker Newt Gingrich.

"Clinton stood up to the Republicans when they wanted to cut those social programmes," said Jay Rank, a social services aide from Milton, Pennsylvania, who supported Republican President George Bush in the 1992 election. "They would have even cut programmes for the mentally retarded. Whoever stood up against that got my vote," he said.
Older voters were particularly scared by Republican attempts to slow the growth of spending on Medicare and Medicaid programmes for senior citizens, the poor and sick.

"I figure Dole might cut off people's Medicare and Medicaid. I think he's going to cut off the old people and I want to stop him," said Mazie Wells, a retired woman from Crewe, Virginia who voted for Bush in 1992.
Even some who intend to vote for Republicans for Congress and like Dole personally are supporting Clinton to prevent changes they fear may be too drastic.

"I'd like to see a check in the system and that happens with Clinton working with a Republican Congress. It makes people think a lot clearer in terms of what they can get done," said Joe Braun, a Cleveland computer technician.

Mike Donnellan, an engineering consultant in the Atlanta suburbs, said that by voting for Clinton for president and Republicans for Congress he wanted to keep either side from enacting what he regarded as their extremist agendas.
"I think Dole is a good, honest and ethical man. My concern is he would be the rubber stamp for the Republican Congress," he said.

Like several others, Donnellan also expressed doubts about Dole's age of 73. "There are issues of technology -- the proper use and distribution of new technology. I don't think Dole gets it," he said.

"I'm a registered Republican but I think Dole is too old," said Beulah McDonald, a homemaker in Campbellsville Kentucky, who said she had still not forgiven Republicans for last year's shutdowns of the federal government in a budget confrontation with Clinton.

Ruby Bovik, a Republican real estate agent from Austin, Texas, who supports Dole said his main problem was his age. "Dole is not a charismatic person. The American public, especially the younger generation, is impressed by charisma, a full head of hair, straight teeth, a nice smile," she said.
In Western states, the environment is a particularly strong issue that has become a loser for Dole.
"I've leaned towards the Republicans in recent years but I'm scared of too much deregulation on the environment," said Kathryn Ann Kobza, a homemaker in Ridgefield, Washington.

"I really and truly don't think our environmental problems will solve themselves if we're all given free rein to do whatever we want," said Kobza, who voted for Bush in 1992 but plans to back Clinton this year.

Up the coast in Tacoma, Washington, Mariel Puscar voted for Texan Ross Perot last time but supports Clinton now. "I like Clinton's attitude towards Medicare. Dole is too conservative for me," she said.
Of the 1992 Perot voters in the sample, all but one had abandoned him this year.
"Perot was sort of a disappointment to me. I don't think he's stable enough for the job," said Robert Perkins, a retired auto dealer in Charleston, South Carolina who is backing Dole this time.
Then there is the economy, still rolling ahead creating new jobs.

"I'm doing better under Clinton than I ever did under any Republican. So is my husband. It would take something amazing to change my mind," said Cynthia Logue, a tarot card reader from Marion, Arkansas.
